extracted.intended_audience: academic researchers, empirical IP scholars, and policy makers interested in patent examination quality and USPTO processes
extracted.subtask_description: Use micro-level patent application and examiner data to assess how allocated examination time and examiner promotions affect granting behavior and the quality/value of issued patents. The paper operationalizes legal standards, prosecution events, examiner behavior, and value proxies to test causal relationships.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patentability requirements (35 U.S.C. §§101, 102, 103, 112)
rubrics_metrics.description: An examiner must assess whether claimed inventions meet statutory requirements: subject matter/utility (35 U.S.C. §101), novelty (35 U.S.C. §102), non-obviousness (35 U.S.C. §103), and disclosure/written-description/enablement (35 U.S.C. §112).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The paper emphasizes that lack-of-novelty (§102) and obviousness (§103) rejections require comparison with prior art and thus require examiners to conduct prior art searches; obviousness rejections are especially time-consuming because they may require combining multiple references and articulating why the combination would make the claim obvious. If the examiner fails to set forth a basis of rejection, the application must be allowed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examination-time allocations
rubrics_metrics.description: The Patent Office sets expected hours per application that vary by technology area and by examiner GS pay grade; higher GS levels are allocated fewer hours to review an application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Promotions to higher GS levels are roughly equated to a 10–15% decrease in allocated hours per grade; example table shows compound tools (GS-7: 19.7 hrs → GS-14: 10.2 hrs) and artificial intelligence (GS-7: 45.1 hrs → GS-14: 23.4 hrs). Time allocations are a primary mechanism hypothesized to affect examiner scrutiny and grant rates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grant rate (incidence of granted patent)
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether an application is allowed (granted) by the examiner; the paper measures grant incidence for each application (sample overall ~68%).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Grant rates are the key outcome. The analysis documents within-examiner increases in grant rates following promotions that reduce allocated time (e.g., moving from GS-7 to GS-14 associated with a 9–19 percentage-point increase, or roughly 13–28% higher). Grant-rate changes are interpreted under the assumption that sufficiently timed exams yield correct determinations on average.

rubrics_metrics.name: Incidence of rejections by statutory basis (§101, §102, §103, §112)
rubrics_metrics.description: For each application, record whether at least one claim was rejected on each statutory ground: §101 (subject matter/utility), §102 (novelty), §103 (obviousness), §112 (disclosure).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sample incidence: ~10% §101, 56% §102, 72% §103, 36% §112. The paper focuses on how the probability of each rejection type changes with reductions in allotted examination time, noting obviousness rejections are particularly time-intensive and more likely to fall with less time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examiner prior-art search intensity (share of examiner-originated citations)
rubrics_metrics.description: Proxy for how intensively an examiner searches prior art: the share of prior art references cited in an issued patent that originate from the examiner (vs. disclosed by applicant).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used as an outcome to infer search effort; previous work suggests examiner-originated citations are more likely associated with rejections. The paper reports sample statistics (e.g., mean share ~0.545 for issued patents) and shows examiner promotions that reduce time are associated with decreases in examiner-originated citations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Post-issuance patent quality/value proxies (renewal, forward citations, generality)
rubrics_metrics.description: Measures used to proxy patent value and quality: incidence of patent renewal at 4 and 8 years, forward-looking citations normalized by number of claims, and patent generality score (1 minus Herfindahl index of technological concentration of forward citations).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Renewals indicate commercial value (sample renewals: 4-year ~0.886, 8-year ~0.716). Forward citations and generality indicate scholarly/technological impact and breadth. The paper tests whether patents issued by time-constrained examiners are lower on these proxies (finding decreases). Forward citations are corrected/truncated by technology and results are robust to inclusion of technology-by-year fixed effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Random assignment of applications within Art Units
rubrics_metrics.description: Applications are (generally) randomly assigned by the Supervisory Patent Examiner (SPE) to individual examiners within an Art Unit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Random (or effectively random) assignment supports causal inference by reducing applicant-facing selection into examiners; SPE non-random assignments occur but reportedly not based on characteristics affecting patentability (e.g., assignments based on examiner backlog). The paper relies on this to justify identification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examiner fixed-effects identification strategy
rubrics_metrics.description: Follow individual examiners over time and use examiner fixed effects to control for time-invariant examiner heterogeneity in granting tendencies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fixed effects isolate within-examiner changes (e.g., around promotions that reduce time) so that inherent differences across examiners (including promotion-seeking disposition) do not drive results. Standard errors clustered at examiner level. The approach helps decouple GS-level/time-allocation effects from unobserved examiner traits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Control for experience (years) and separation from GS-level effects
rubrics_metrics.description: Include experience indicators (in multi-year bins) and, in some specifications, nest experience within GS-levels to separately identify experience (tenure) effects from promotion/GS-level (time-allocation) effects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Experience is included in 2-year bins (0–1, 2–3, 4–5, etc.) to break the age/cohort/year collinearity and to examine inverse-U empirical patterns; some specifications find inverse-U between experience and grant rates while discrete jumps occur at promotions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Technology-by-year fixed effects and application covariates
rubrics_metrics.description: Include interactions of technology subcategories with year fixed effects (37 NBER tech sub-categories) and application covariates (applicant entity size, filing-to-disposition time and its square) to control for time-varying technological trends and application-level confounders.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These controls address concerns that examiners are reassigned across technologies with promotions or that tech-specific citation/renewal patterns change over time. Robustness checks show results are stable to these additions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Signatory authority and scrutiny changes (partial/full signatory)
rubrics_metrics.description: Within-GS variation: GS‑13 examiners may obtain partial signatory authority (reduced time allotment and ability to sign off on first actions) and GS‑14 examiners have full signatory authority; below GS‑13 examiners require review by a signatory examiner.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Promotions that alter signatory status change both time allocations and the level of secondary scrutiny. Because some time-reducing promotions do not change scrutiny, this variation strengthens identification separating time-allocation effects from scrutiny changes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Data and sample construction requirements (PAIR and FOIA rosters)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use application-level PAIR data on all utility patent applications filed on or after March 2001 and disposed by July 2012; match applications to examiner rosters obtained via FOIA to determine examiner identity, GS-level, and experience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Data collection required extensive scraping/aggregation across PAIR pages and PDFs; fuzzy name matching used for rosters; define the examiner as the individual who did majority of work (non-signatory when both non-signatory and signatory present; otherwise signatory). Continuations are treated as new applications; RCEs are not treated as new applications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Outcome measurement treatment of continuations and RCEs
rubrics_metrics.description: Classify prosecution events carefully: continuation applications (historical form) are treated as rejection/abandonment of original and filing of a new application; Request for Continued Examination (RCE) keeps the same serial number and examiner and is not treated as a new application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This classification affects measured grant rates and interpretation: the reported grant/incidence rates over the sample reflect this counting rule and therefore may differ from 'original application eventually allowed' metrics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Average examiner time-per-application (empirical benchmark)
rubrics_metrics.description: An empirical benchmark used: examiners spend on average nineteen hours reviewing an application (reading, searching, comparing art, writing actions, responding, and interviews).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This benchmark motivates the plausibility that allocated hours are binding; small absolute reductions in allotted hours can materially affect ability to perform time-intensive tasks (e.g., obviousness rejections). The paper cites a 2010 PTO-commissioned report where examiners expressed need for more time.
